blocks.text:
Design a web crawler, the system that starts from a handful of seed URLs and follows links outward across the web, discovering and fetching pages at massive scale for something like a search engine's index to be built from. The two problems that make this genuinely hard are not fetching pages themselves, which is simple in isolation, but knowing whether a URL has already been crawled before out of a set that can grow into the tens of billions, and behaving politely toward every individual website along the way, since a crawler that hits one site's server too fast will either get itself blocked or, worse, actually degrade that site for its real visitors.

The technique that makes tracking billions of seen URLs affordable is a Bloom filter, a compact structure that can say "definitely never seen" with total certainty or "probably already seen" with a small, tunable chance of being wrong, using a small, fixed amount of memory per URL regardless of how many URLs have been added.

The two problems that make this genuinely hard are not fetching pages themselves, which is simple in isolation, but knowing whether a URL has already been crawled before out of a set that can grow into the tens of billions, and behaving politely toward every individual website along the way, since a crawler that hits one site's server too fast will either get itself blocked or, worse, actually degrade that site for its real visitors.

The technique that makes tracking billions of seen URLs affordable is a Bloom filter, a compact structure that can say "definitely never seen" with total certainty or "probably already seen" with a small, tunable chance of being wrong, using a small, fixed amount of memory per URL regardless of how many URLs have been added.

blocks.text: Starting from a set of seed URLs, the crawler should discover and fetch linked pages recursively. It should respect each site's robots.txt rules, honoring which paths are disallowed for crawling. It should rate-limit itself per domain, never hammering any single site faster than a configured, polite rate. It should avoid re-fetching a URL it has already crawled recently, and periodically revisit pages to pick up content changes over time. Fetched content should be stored for a downstream indexing pipeline to consume.

blocks.text: Five qualities matter here, and the first two are in genuine tension with each other.

blocks.alt: Scalable seen-URL tracking, politeness, massive parallelism, reasonable freshness, and a fault-tolerant frontier

blocks.text: Seen-URL tracking has to scale to billions of discovered URLs without needing a full, exact record stored for every single one. Politeness matters because a crawler is a guest on every site it visits, and violating that trust gets a crawler blocked outright, which defeats its entire purpose. Massive parallelism is needed to make any real dent in the size of the web at all, but it has to coexist with per-domain politeness, since many workers crawling many domains must never collectively slam any one domain harder than a single well-behaved crawler would. Freshness here means periodic revisits on a reasonable schedule, not real-time updates the moment a page changes. And the frontier, the queue of URLs still waiting to be crawled, needs to survive individual worker crashes without silently losing whatever that worker was in the middle of processing.

blocks.text: This design assumes a Bloom filter is acceptable for seen-URL tracking, meaning a small, rare chance of a false positive causing a genuinely new URL to be skipped is tolerable at this scale, in exchange for the enormous memory savings worked out in section 6. Politeness is enforced through both robots.txt compliance and an internal per-domain rate limiter, whichever is stricter. JavaScript rendering is out of scope, this design fetches and parses raw HTML only. A maximum crawl depth and per-domain page budget guard against crawler traps, covered further in section 21.

blocks.text: Over its lifetime, a crawl at real scale might discover tens of billions of distinct URLs. A Bloom filter tuned for a low false positive rate needs roughly ten bits per entry, which for ten billion URLs comes out to about twelve gigabytes, a size that comfortably fits in memory on a modest number of machines. Storing every URL string exactly instead, even at a modest fifty bytes per URL average length, would need several times that much space just for the raw strings, before any indexing structure on top. Across the whole fetcher fleet, a real crawl might sustain thousands of page fetches per second, spread thin across an enormous number of individual domains so that no single site ever sees more than its fair, polite share of that traffic.

blocks.alt: Tens of billions of URLs discovered over the crawl's lifetime, roughly ten bits per URL in a tuned Bloom filter, several times more space needed to store full URL strings exactly instead, and thousands of fetches per second across the whole fleet

blocks.text: Seed URLs enter a frontier that is partitioned by domain, and a pool of fetcher workers continuously dequeues URLs from it. Before fetching, a worker checks that domain's cached robots.txt rules and consults a per-domain rate limiter, only proceeding once both agree the fetch is currently allowed. A fetched page's content goes to durable storage for downstream indexing, and its outbound links are extracted and checked against a Bloom filter, with probably-new URLs enqueued back into the frontier to continue the crawl outward.

blocks.text: A newly discovered URL is run through several independent hash functions, each pointing at one bit in a large, shared bit array. If any of those bits is not yet set, the URL is definitely new, since a previously-seen URL would have set every one of those same bits already. If every bit happens to already be set, the URL is treated as probably already seen, which is either genuinely true or, occasionally, a coincidental overlap with other URLs' bits, a false positive. Crucially, this can never produce a false negative, a URL that was truly already seen will always have every one of its bits set.

blocks.alt: A URL hashes to several bits in a shared array; any unset bit proves the URL is definitely new, while all bits being set means it is probably already seen, with a small, bounded chance of a false positive

blocks.text: Before any fetch, the rate limiter checks how long it has been since that specific domain was last fetched, allowing the request only once a configured minimum delay has passed.
blocks.content: Before any fetch, the rate limiter checks how long it has been since that specific domain was last fetched, allowing the request only once a configured minimum delay has passed.

blocks.alt: A fetch is allowed once enough time has passed since the last fetch to that same domain, and otherwise made to wait, regardless of how many other domains are being fetched concurrently

blocks.text: Most of this system's complexity is internal, between the frontier, fetchers, and the Bloom filter, rather than exposed through a rich external API, since a crawler is largely a closed, continuously-running pipeline rather than a request-response service.

blocks.alt: Domain, tracking cached robots.txt rules and last fetch time, and CrawledPage, tracking each page's last crawl time and a content hash for change detection

blocks.text: CrawledPage's contentHash lets a later re-crawl cheaply detect whether a page actually changed since last visited, without needing to compare the full content byte for byte.
blocks.content: CrawledPage's contentHash lets a later re-crawl cheaply detect whether a page actually changed since last visited, without needing to compare the full content byte for byte.

blocks.text: The Bloom filter itself is not a database table at all, it is an in-memory (or memory-mapped) bit array, chosen specifically because a real database row per URL, even a minimal one, would cost far more space than this problem can afford at billions of entries. The durable Domain and CrawledPage tables exist for the comparatively small amount of state that genuinely needs to be exact, robots.txt rules and per-page metadata, while the sheer volume of "have I seen this URL" checks is handled entirely by the approximate structure.

blocks.alt: A fetcher checks politeness, fetches the page, extracts links, checks each against the Bloom filter, and enqueues the probably-new ones
A fetch attempted too soon after the last one to the same domain is blocked and retried later, rather than proceeding immediately

blocks.text: The happy path is exactly the fetch flow above, politeness allows the fetch, the page is retrieved, and its links feed back into the frontier. The workflow worth walking through separately is what happens when a fetcher discovers a URL the Bloom filter reports as probably already seen but which was, in fact, never actually crawled, a false positive. That URL is simply never re-added to the frontier, and the crawl proceeds as if it genuinely had already been visited. This is exactly the trade this design accepts: an occasional, rare page never gets crawled at all, in exchange for the massive memory savings that make tracking billions of URLs affordable in the first place.

blocks.alt: A domain's robots.txt is fetched once and cached, reused for every subsequent page on that domain rather than re-fetched each time

blocks.text: This caching matters for the same reason per-domain rate limiting does, fetching robots.txt before every single page on a domain would itself be an impolite, wasteful multiplication of requests to that site.

blocks.alt: The frontier behaves like an acknowledgment-based queue, redelivering a URL to another worker if the one holding it crashes before confirming it was fully processed

blocks.text: Treating the frontier as a proper acknowledged queue, rather than a plain in-memory list, is what makes a fetcher worker crash a recoverable event instead of quietly losing whatever URL it was working on.
blocks.content: Treating the frontier as a proper acknowledged queue, rather than a plain in-memory list, is what makes a fetcher worker crash a recoverable event instead of quietly losing whatever URL it was working on.

blocks.alt: A URL is routed to a fetcher worker by hashing its domain, so every URL for one domain consistently lands on the same worker, keeping that worker solely responsible for enforcing that domain's politeness

blocks.text: Partitioning by domain rather than round-robin is what lets politeness be enforced correctly without needing cross-worker coordination, since only one worker is ever touching a given domain's rate limit state at a time.
blocks.content: Partitioning by domain rather than round-robin is what lets politeness be enforced correctly without needing cross-worker coordination, since only one worker is ever touching a given domain's rate limit state at a time.

blocks.alt: A growing frontier backlog triggers adding more fetcher workers to drain it faster

blocks.text: Scaling out fetcher workers increases how many distinct domains can be crawled concurrently, without threatening any single domain's politeness, since the domain-partitioned routing from section 16 keeps each domain's traffic isolated to one worker regardless of total fleet size.

blocks.text: The Content Store scales the ordinary way large content stores do, partitioned by domain or URL hash, since crawled pages are large, mostly-immutable blobs with no need for complex cross-page querying at write time.

blocks.alt: Whether a URL has been seen before is probabilistic, tolerating a rare false positive; how fresh a page's content is stays eventually consistent, refreshed on a schedule rather than in real time

blocks.text: Neither piece of state in this system demands strong, exact consistency, which is exactly what allows both the Bloom filter's space savings and a comparatively relaxed re-crawl scheduling policy.
blocks.content: Neither piece of state in this system demands strong, exact consistency, which is exactly what allows both the Bloom filter's space savings and a comparatively relaxed re-crawl scheduling policy.

blocks.alt: If a fetcher crashes mid-fetch without acknowledging its URL, the frontier notices the missing acknowledgment and redelivers that URL to a different worker

blocks.text: This acknowledgment-based redelivery is what keeps a single worker crash from silently dropping whatever URLs it was in the middle of processing, the same durability guarantee an ordinary message queue provides, applied here to crawl work instead of application messages.
blocks.content: This acknowledgment-based redelivery is what keeps a single worker crash from silently dropping whatever URLs it was in the middle of processing, the same durability guarantee an ordinary message queue provides, applied here to crawl work instead of application messages.

blocks.alt: A page generating an unusually large number of new links against one domain's safety limits stops the crawler from following it deeper; otherwise crawling continues normally

blocks.text: Respecting robots.txt is as much a legal and ethical boundary as a technical one, ignoring it risks real consequences for whoever operates the crawler. Separately, crawler traps, pages engineered or accidentally structured to generate a near-infinite stream of new links, such as an auto-generated calendar with a "next month" link on every page, need an explicit safety valve, a maximum crawl depth or page budget per domain, since nothing about the crawl logic itself would otherwise stop it from spinning forever on one trap.

blocks.text: Frontier backlog size and growth rate is the clearest signal of whether the fetcher fleet is keeping pace with discovery. The Bloom filter's estimated false positive rate is worth tracking too, since it climbs as more URLs are added and eventually needs a larger filter or a periodic rebuild to stay within an acceptable bound. Per-domain fetch failure rates help catch both broken sites and crawler behavior that a site's own defenses have started blocking.

blocks.alt: One unusually large domain dominating a worker's entire time budget, the Bloom filter's false positive rate creeping up as more URLs accumulate, and a crawler trap generating unbounded links from a single page

blocks.text: The first of these is directly mitigated by per-domain politeness itself, a rate-limited domain cannot monopolize a worker's attention no matter how many pages it has, since the worker is forced to wait between fetches regardless of backlog size.

blocks.text: A Bloom filter is the right default because its one weakness, a rare false positive, quietly skipping a page that would eventually be found again through some other link anyway, is far less costly than either the memory bill of exact tracking or the wasted fetch capacity of not tracking seen URLs at all.

blocks.text: The Bloom filter's memory savings, worked out in section 6, are themselves the single largest cost optimization in this entire design. Beyond that, caching robots.txt per domain and enforcing politeness both reduce wasted, redundant fetch traffic, and partitioning the frontier by domain avoids needing expensive cross-worker coordination just to keep politeness correct.

["A crawler trap generates effectively unlimited new links from one page, correctly halted by a per-domain depth or page budget rather than crawled indefinitely.","A robots.txt file disallows crawling entirely, correctly resulting in zero pages fetched from that domain rather than a partial, rule-violating crawl.","A redirect chain leads a URL through several intermediate hops before reaching its final destination, requiring the crawler to follow it while still respecting an overall maximum redirect count.","A dynamic page returns meaningfully different content on every fetch, which content-hash-based change detection correctly treats as a genuine change each time rather than assuming a bug."]
items: A crawler trap generates effectively unlimited new links from one page, correctly halted by a per-domain depth or page budget rather than crawled indefinitely.
A robots.txt file disallows crawling entirely, correctly resulting in zero pages fetched from that domain rather than a partial, rule-violating crawl.
A redirect chain leads a URL through several intermediate hops before reaching its final destination, requiring the crawler to follow it while still respecting an overall maximum redirect count.
A dynamic page returns meaningfully different content on every fetch, which content-hash-based change detection correctly treats as a genuine change each time rather than assuming a bug.

blocks.text: Rolling out a change to politeness timing or robots.txt parsing needs careful, gradual deployment, since a bug there risks the crawler either getting itself blocked across many sites at once or, worse, actually degrading real websites' service to their genuine visitors. Bloom filter resizing, needed as the false positive rate creeps upward over the crawl's lifetime, should be planned as a deliberate, monitored migration rather than an emergency response to an already-degraded rate.

blocks.text: JavaScript rendering support would let the crawler see dynamically generated content that a raw HTML fetch misses entirely, at real additional compute cost per page. Smarter, change-frequency-aware re-crawl scheduling, revisiting fast-changing pages more often than static ones, would make better use of limited fetch capacity than a uniform revisit schedule.

items: Architecture: a domain-partitioned, acknowledgment-based frontier feeding fetcher workers that enforce robots.txt and per-domain rate limits, with discovered links deduplicated through a Bloom filter.

Capacity: tens of billions of discovered URLs, roughly ten bits per URL in a tuned Bloom filter against several times more space for storing full URL strings exactly, and thousands of fetches per second across the fleet.
The core techniques: a Bloom filter for space-efficient seen-URL tracking, and a per-domain rate limiter for politeness, both worked through with a real, verified implementation.
Database: a comparatively small durable footprint, since the bulk of seen-URL tracking deliberately lives in an approximate, in-memory structure rather than a database table.
End-to-end workflows: a normal fetch and a politeness-blocked fetch, both traced as sequence diagrams.
Consistency: probabilistic seen-URL tracking and eventually-refreshed page freshness, neither one needing strong, exact guarantees.
Trade-offs: exact hash-set tracking versus a Bloom filter versus no seen-URL tracking at all, compared directly on memory cost, false negative risk, and where each breaks down.
